Satan seized, bound and sealed in the Abyss for a thousand years
Thrones, the martyrs who came to life and reigned: the first resurrection
Satan released; Gog and Magog; fire from heaven; the devil cast into the lake of fire
The great white throne: books opened, the dead judged, the second death

Jewish apocalyptic had already imagined the binding of evil powers in a pit until the day of judgment. In 1 Enoch 10:4-6 the archangel Raphael binds the fallen watcher Azazel hand and foot, throws him into darkness, covers him with rough stones until the great day, and then he is to be cast into fire; 1 Enoch 10:11-13 has the other watchers bound for seventy generations beneath the earth. Jubilees 10:7-11 tells of nine-tenths of the evil spirits bound in the place of judgment while a tenth remain with Mastema, the satanic figure. Isaiah 24:21-22 says the host of heaven and kings of the earth will be shut in a prison and 'after many days' be punished. Many Jewish texts also expected a temporary messianic kingdom before the final age: 4 Ezra 7:28-29 assigns it 400 years, after which the Messiah dies and the world returns to primeval silence before the resurrection; 2 Baruch 29-30 and 40:3 picture a messianic reign 'until the world of corruption is ended'; and a 'world-week' scheme (six days of a thousand years each followed by a sabbath, derived from Psalm 90:4 and Genesis 1-2) appears in the Epistle of Barnabas 15 and, in disputed form, 2 Enoch 32-33. Much later rabbinic discussions (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 97a-99a) offer lengths from 40 to 7,000 years. Ezekiel's sequence — resurrection of Israel (Ezekiel 37), a messianic reign, the onslaught of Gog of Magog (38-39) and the new temple-city (40-48) — supplies the order of Revelation 20-22.

Greco-Roman readers would hear other notes. Rome's propaganda spoke of an 'eternal city' and a golden age restored under Augustus (Virgil, Eclogue 4); John's thousand-year reign belongs instead to Christ and his martyrs. The martyrs are described as 'beheaded with the axe' (pelekus), the old Roman method of execution for citizens, while thrones and judgment scenes evoked the tribunal (bēma) of Roman governors before whom Christians were tried. The early church divided over the passage: Papias, Justin Martyr (Dialogue 80-81), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36) and Tertullian held to an earthly millennial kingdom after Christ's return (chiliasm), while Origen, Tyconius and Augustine (City of God 20.7-9) read the thousand years as the present church age, the view that dominated medieval and Reformation teaching. Postmillennialism (developed among Puritans and popularised by Daniel Whitby and Jonathan Edwards), modern historic premillennialism (Ladd) and dispensational premillennialism (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord) all grew from the same text.
An angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss

The Abyss (Greek abyssos) translates the Hebrew tehom, the deep of Genesis 1:2, and in Second Temple literature becomes the prison of fallen spirits (1 Enoch 10:4-6; 18:11-16; 21:7-10; Jubilees 5:6-10). Isaiah 22:22 gives the key of the house of David to Eliakim. The demons in Luke 8:31 beg not to be sent into the Abyss.
Keys signified delegated authority to open and shut — a steward's or gatekeeper's office in Roman households and temples.

Christ holds the keys of death and Hades (1:18); the angel acts on his authority. The Abyss earlier released the locusts (9:1-11) and the beast (11:7; 17:8); now the source of evil is itself locked up.
Holding in his hand a great chain

1 Enoch 54:3-5 describes iron chains of immeasurable weight prepared for the hosts of Azazel; 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 speak of angels kept in 'chains of gloom'. Isaiah 24:22 pictures rulers gathered as prisoners in a pit.
Chains and fetters were standard in Roman custody; prisoners of war were led in chains in triumphal processions.
A symbol of effective restraint. No one supposes a spiritual being is bound with metal; the question is the scope of the restraint.
The dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan

Combines the serpent of Eden (Genesis 3:1-15), the sea-dragon Leviathan/Rahab (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13-14), the accuser (satan) of Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3, and the slanderer (diabolos, the Septuagint's word for satan). Wisdom of Solomon 2:24 says death entered the world through the devil's envy.
Python, the dragon slain by Apollo, and other chaos-dragon myths were well known in Asia Minor; emperors were sometimes associated with Apollo the dragon-slayer.

The full title repeats 12:9 exactly, signalling that the defeated accuser of chapter 12 is now dealt with. Many see the deliberate link as evidence that 20:1-3 relates to the same victory as 12:7-11 (Christ's death and exaltation).
He seized the dragon… and bound him… so that he could not deceive the nations

1 Enoch 10:4-6 (Raphael binds Azazel in the darkness until the day of judgment, then he is cast into fire) is the nearest parallel; Jubilees 10:7-11 binds most of Mastema's spirits; Tobit 8:3 binds the demon Asmodeus; Testament of Levi 18:12 expects the new priest to bind Beliar; Testament of Moses 10:1 says the devil will have an end. Isaiah 24:21-22 imprisons cosmic powers 'for many days'.

The purpose clause is specific: Satan is restrained 'so that he could not deceive the nations' any longer. Jesus spoke of binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29; Mark 3:27), of Satan falling (Luke 10:18) and being cast out at the cross (John 12:31-32). Whether Revelation 20 describes that same victory or a future, total confinement is the central exegetical debate of the millennium.

Amillennialists (Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Storms) see a binding accomplished at Christ's first coming: Satan is not inactive (1 Peter 5:8) but restrained in one specific respect — he cannot prevent the gospel going to the nations or gather them for the final assault until the end. They link 'bind' (deō) to Matthew 12:29 and the casting down of 12:9.

Postmillennialists (Gentry, Mathison, Warfield) agree the binding began with Christ's victory and stress its historical effect: the nations, once deceived, are progressively discipled through the gospel, so that the binding underwrites the gospel's expected success in history.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Waymeyer) argue that the language of seizing, binding, throwing, shutting and sealing describes complete removal from earthly activity, which does not match the New Testament picture of Satan's present activity (Acts 5:3; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 Peter 5:8); the binding therefore follows Christ's return.

Historic premillennialists (Ladd) likewise see a future, total binding after the Second Coming, though Ladd granted that Christ's first coming inaugurated a real but partial defeat of Satan; the millennium is a further stage of the kingdom's victory in history.

Older historicists often dated the binding to the overthrow of pagan Rome under Constantine (fourth century), when the devil was dethroned from the empire; others (Elliott, many nineteenth-century writers) expected it still in the future.
A thousand years

Psalm 90:4 (a thousand years as a day) underlies a 'world-week' scheme in which history runs six thousand-year days followed by a sabbath millennium (Epistle of Barnabas 15; disputed in 2 Enoch 32-33). Jubilees 4:29-30 says Adam died seventy years short of a thousand, fulfilling 'in the day you eat… you shall die'. Temporary messianic kingdoms appear in 4 Ezra 7:28-29 (400 years) and 2 Baruch 40:3; later rabbinic debates (Talmud Sanhedrin 97a-99a, late material) propose 40, 70, 365, 400, 1,000, 2,000 or 7,000 years. Deuteronomy 7:9 promises covenant love to a thousand generations.
Roman ideology celebrated the 'eternal city' and a returning golden age under Augustus; secular games marked new saeculum cycles of roughly a century.

The phrase occurs six times in 20:2-7. Interpreters divide over whether it is a literal span or a symbolic number (10 x 10 x 10, a complete and long period) — though some literalists and some symbolists agree on chronology but not on duration, and vice versa. The key questions are when it occurs relative to Christ's return, where the reign takes place (heaven or earth), and who reigns.

Postmillennialists see a long era (not necessarily 1,000 literal years) of Christ's reign from heaven, during which the gospel wins the great majority of the world and brings unprecedented righteousness and peace before his return. Some (Warfield) see it as the bliss of the saints in heaven during the gospel age; others (Gentry) as the whole inter-advent period with growing triumph.

Amillennialists (Augustine, Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Beale) understand the thousand years as a symbol for the whole period between Christ's first and second comings, during which deceased believers reign with Christ in heaven and the church on earth lives under his reign.

Historic premillennialists (Ladd, Blomberg, the early chiliasts Justin and Irenaeus) hold that after Christ's return there will be an earthly reign of Christ with his resurrected saints, of long and perhaps not literally 1,000-year duration, before the final state.

Dispensational premillennialists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) expect a literal 1,000-year earthly kingdom after the Second Coming, centred on Jerusalem, fulfilling God's unconditional promises to national Israel alongside blessing for the nations.

Full preterists (Max King, Don Preston) usually identify the millennium with the transitional period between the cross and AD 70 (often c. 40 years), ending in the 'end of the age' and the final judgment they place at the fall of Jerusalem. This view is outside historic creedal orthodoxy because it denies a future bodily resurrection; proponents reply that Scripture's time texts require it.
He threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him
Daniel's lions' den was sealed with the king's signet (Daniel 6:17); 1 Enoch 10:5 covers Azazel's pit with rough stones. Jesus' tomb was sealed (Matthew 27:66).
A seal impressed in clay or wax over a door or container guaranteed it against tampering on the authority of its owner.
A heaping-up of verbs underlines that the restraint is real and secure. The irony may be intended: the powers sealed Christ's tomb, but now Christ's angel seals Satan's prison.
Dispensationalists and many premillennialists argue that shutting and sealing the Abyss over Satan means total removal from the earth, which cannot describe the present age.

Amillennialists answer that apocalyptic prison imagery expresses decisive restriction on a stated activity (deceiving the nations), just as the 'chains' of Jude 6 do not prevent fallen angels from all activity.
After that, he must be released for a brief period of time

Isaiah 24:22 says the imprisoned powers will be punished 'after many days'. Daniel 7:12 notes beasts whose lives were prolonged for a season. In 4 Ezra 7:29-30 the messianic age ends and the world reverts before the judgment.

'Must' (Greek dei) signals divine purpose: even evil's final outburst serves God's plan, exposing the heart of the unrepentant. The 'short time' parallels the devil's short time in 12:12 and the 3½-year motifs, suggesting to many a brief final intensification of opposition.
Amillennialists and many postmillennialists equate the release with the final apostasy and the 'man of lawlessness' (2 Thessalonians 2:3-12) just before Christ returns.
Dispensationalists see a final test of humanity at the end of the earthly millennium: even under Christ's perfect rule, people born during the kingdom rebel when given the opportunity.
I saw the thrones, and those seated on them had been given authority to judge

Daniel 7:9 ('thrones were set in place'), 7:22 (judgment given in favour of the saints of the Most High, who then possess the kingdom) and 7:27. Jesus promised the Twelve thrones to judge the tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30); Paul says the saints will judge the world and angels (1 Corinthians 6:2-3). Wisdom of Solomon 3:8 says the righteous will judge nations.
Christians were judged before Roman tribunals (bēma) seated on curule chairs; the reversal is complete when the condemned sit on thrones.

The scene enacts Daniel 7:22: the verdict goes in favour of the saints, and they share in Christ's rule. Who sits on the thrones (the martyrs, all saints, the apostles, or the twenty-four elders) and where the thrones are (heaven, as every other throne in Revelation except Satan's and the beast's, or earth) are disputed.
Amillennialists observe that of 47 uses of 'throne' in Revelation almost all are in heaven, and so locate this reign in heaven with the souls of deceased believers during the present age.
Dispensationalists locate the thrones on earth, after Christ's return, sharing his reign over the nations from Jerusalem (Revelation 5:10, 'they will reign on the earth').
Postmillennialists (e.g. Gentry) often see believers on earth and in heaven reigning with Christ as his kingdom advances, the thrones expressing the saints' vindication and royal-priestly calling.
The souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God

The souls under the altar (6:9-11) cried for vindication; Jewish martyr traditions (2 Maccabees 7; 4 Maccabees) promised the faithful dead vindication and life. Daniel 12:2-3 promises that the wise will shine.
The verb (pelekizō) refers to execution with an axe, the traditional Roman capital punishment, later largely replaced by the sword; tradition says Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded.

The martyrs who cried 'how long?' are now enthroned. The same people 'had not worshipped the beast', so the group may be all faithful believers (in principle martyrs), or the martyrs plus a wider group (the grammar can be read as two groups). The word 'souls' is pivotal for those who see a heavenly, intermediate-state reign.
Amillennialists stress 'souls' (as in 6:9): John sees disembodied believers alive and reigning with Christ in heaven during the church age.
Premillennialists respond that 'souls' can denote persons and that they are seen after they 'came to life' — that is, resurrected.
Dispensationalists often limit this group to tribulation martyrs (from chapters 6-13) and Old Testament saints raised at Christ's return, the church having been raptured and enthroned earlier.
Those who had not worshiped the beast or its image, and had not received its mark
The three young men of Daniel 3 who refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image are the archetype of faithful refusal.

Refusal to offer incense to the emperor's image could bring death; Pliny's letter to Trajan (Letters 10.96, c. AD 112) shows Christians tested by being asked to invoke the gods and venerate the emperor's statue.
These are the overcomers of the letters and of chapters 13-15. Their reign is the reward promised in 2:26-27 and 3:21.
They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years

Ezekiel 37 (dry bones made to live, followed by a Davidic king and then Gog's attack in Ezekiel 38-39) supplies the sequence; Daniel 12:2 promises awakening of those who sleep in the dust; Isaiah 26:19.

The verb ezēsan ('they lived/came to life') is the hinge. Elsewhere in Revelation it is used of Christ's resurrection (2:8) and of the beast's revival (13:14). Interpreters debate whether it means bodily resurrection or spiritual life (regeneration, or the life of the soul after death).

Ladd and many premillennialists, echoing Henry Alford's famous argument, insist that if 'came to life' in 20:5 means bodily resurrection for 'the rest of the dead', it must mean the same in 20:4; therefore there are two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium.

Dispensationalists (Deere, Walvoord) agree: the verb and context denote bodily resurrection of the righteous before the millennium, completing the 'first resurrection' that began with Christ and the raptured church.

Amillennialists (Hoekema, Kline, Storms) argue the verb describes the believer's entrance into heavenly life at death, which is a 'resurrection' of a different kind from the bodily resurrection of the rest; Kline argues that 'first' in Revelation marks the provisional, pre-consummation order (first heaven, first earth) and so the first resurrection belongs to this age.

Postmillennialists vary: some (Warfield) take it of the intermediate state in heaven; others, following Augustine, take it of regeneration — spiritual resurrection with Christ (John 5:24-25; Ephesians 2:5-6; Colossians 3:1).

Chilton reads the first resurrection as believers' union with Christ in his resurrection (signified in baptism), so that the church reigns now; other partial preterists adopt either the amillennial or postmillennial account.
The rest of the dead did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete

Some Jewish texts envisaged a resurrection of the righteous only or in stages (Psalms of Solomon 3:12; 2 Maccabees 7:14 says there is no resurrection to life for the persecutor; 1 Enoch 51 and 4 Ezra 7:32 envisage a general resurrection).
The verse implies the remaining dead (unbelievers at least) will 'live' after the thousand years for the judgment of 20:12-13. Whether this 'living' is the same kind as in 20:4 is the crux.
Premillennialists see here the clearest evidence for two bodily resurrections, consistent with 'each in his own order' (1 Corinthians 15:23) and 'the resurrection of the righteous' (Luke 14:14).

Amillennialists answer that elsewhere Scripture presents one general resurrection of just and unjust 'in the hour' (John 5:28-29; Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15), and that 20:5a is a parenthesis meaning the rest of the dead did not share in the heavenly life of the saints during the age.
This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy are those who share in it

Jewish writings speak of a resurrection of the righteous (Psalms of Solomon 3:12; 1 Enoch 22; 91:10). 'First resurrection' as a technical term is new with John; its pairing with the 'second death' suggests a symmetry (first resurrection / second death; first death / second resurrection, implied).

The fifth of the book's seven beatitudes. The 'first resurrection' guarantees immunity from the 'second death' and grants a share in Christ's reign and priesthood. Whether it is physical, spiritual, or the believer's transfer to heaven at death is the heart of the millennial debate.

Dispensationalists see the first resurrection as a category occurring in stages — Christ (the firstfruits), the church at the rapture, Old Testament and tribulation saints at the Second Coming — all before the millennium.
Historic premillennialists see one bodily resurrection of believers at Christ's return, before the millennium, followed after it by the resurrection of the rest.
Amillennialists (Kline, Hoekema) see the first resurrection as the believer's death-to-glory transition (or regeneration), with the second, bodily resurrection for all at the end.
Postmillennialists typically follow Augustine (regeneration) or Warfield (the heavenly life of the saints) and see the bodily resurrection of all at the single Second Coming after the millennium.

Full preterists (Max King) read it as the corporate, covenantal resurrection of God's people from the 'death' of the old covenant, completed in AD 70 — a view critics regard as incompatible with the creeds' future bodily resurrection; proponents reply that Paul's resurrection hope was itself framed as Israel's hope (Acts 26:6-8; Romans 11:15) and fulfilled covenantally.
The second death has no power over them

'Second death' appears in the Aramaic Targums (e.g. Targum Onqelos and others on Deuteronomy 33:6, 'let Reuben live and not die the second death'; Targum on Isaiah 22:14; 65:6, 15; Jeremiah 51:39, 57) as final exclusion from the world to come; the Targums' date is debated and some material is later than Revelation, but the phrase evidently circulated in Jewish usage.
Defined in 20:14 and 21:8 as the lake of fire. The promise to Smyrna (2:11) is fulfilled: those who may suffer the first (physical) death for Christ are safe from the second.
They will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with Him

Israel was called to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6); Isaiah 61:6 promises that the restored people will be called priests of the LORD. Daniel 7:27 gives the kingdom to the saints.
In Asia Minor civic priesthoods of the imperial cult were prestigious offices held by local elites; John assigns true priesthood and royalty to faithful believers.

Fulfils 1:6 and 5:10. The saints combine royal and priestly vocations, restoring the role of Adam and Israel. Some see 'reign on the earth' (5:10) as decisive for an earthly millennium; others for a present or eternal reign.
To deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog

Ezekiel 38-39 describes Gog, of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, leading northern hordes against restored Israel and being destroyed on the mountains of Israel. Magog is a son of Japheth (Genesis 10:2). Sibylline Oracles 3.319-322 and 3.512 locate Gog and Magog among distant peoples; 1 Enoch 56:5-8 has Parthians and Medes stirred against the holy land; later rabbinic tradition speaks of 'the war of Gog and Magog' preceding or following the messianic age (e.g. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Numbers 11:26, of late date). Josephus (Antiquities 1.123) identified Magog with the Scythians.
Scythians and other northern 'barbarians' stood for the uncivilised edge of the world in Greek and Roman thought; Rome feared the Parthians to the east.

John universalises Ezekiel's northern invader: Gog and Magog are no longer a single nation but the nations from the four corners of the earth. The name signals the final, total assault on God's people and its instant defeat.

Dispensationalists see a final rebellion at the close of the literal millennium; many (Walvoord) distinguish it from Ezekiel 38-39, which they place earlier (before or during the tribulation), noting differences in setting.

Amillennialists (Beale, White) take 20:8-9 as the same final battle as 16:14 and 19:19, all based on Ezekiel 38-39 and all called 'the war' — evidence that chapter 20 recapitulates rather than follows chapter 19.
Postmillennialists see a brief, late apostasy after the long gospel triumph, crushed by Christ at his return — an assault on a church that has filled the earth ('the broad expanse of the earth').
Various historicists have identified Gog and Magog with specific powers — the Turks, Russia, or other enemies of Christendom — to arise after the millennium or in their own era.
Full preterists commonly identify Gog and Magog with the forces besieging Jerusalem or the persecuting powers of AD 66-70, so that the whole chapter was fulfilled in the first century.
Their number is like the sand of the seashore
The phrase describes the innumerable descendants promised to Abraham (Genesis 22:17; 32:12) but also the vast Canaanite armies arrayed against Israel (Joshua 11:4; Judges 7:12; 1 Samuel 13:5).

An ironic inversion: a promise of blessing is applied to the hostile hordes. It also links with the dragon standing on the sand of the sea (12:17/13:1). The numbers stress how widespread the final rebellion is, raising questions for postmillennial optimism that interpreters answer differently.
They surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city

'Camp' (parembolē) recalls Israel encamped in the wilderness around the tabernacle (Numbers 2; Deuteronomy 23:14); the Qumran War Scroll organises the sons of light in camps. God loves the gates of Zion (Psalm 87:2; 78:68). Ezekiel 38:12 places Gog's attack on the people at the centre of the earth.

The people of God are a pilgrim army (camp) and a city at once — a combined image of the wilderness church and the holy city. Whether this is literal Jerusalem or the people of God worldwide is disputed.
Dispensationalists understand the beloved city as literal Jerusalem, capital of the millennial kingdom, with the saints encamped around it.
Amillennialists and idealists see the worldwide church, the true Zion (Hebrews 12:22), besieged in the final persecution — spread across 'the broad expanse of the earth'.
Postmillennialists likewise read it as the church, which by this stage has filled the earth, surrounded by a last rebellion.
Fire came down from heaven and consumed them
God rains fire and sulfur on Gog (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6); Elijah calls down fire on the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10-12); fire falls on Sodom (Genesis 19:24).
There is no battle — only immediate divine intervention. The ease of victory matches 19:20-21. The false prophet's counterfeit fire from heaven (13:13) is answered by real fire from God.
The lake of fire and sulfur… tormented day and night forever and ever

Gehenna derives from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31-32) and later a symbol of final judgment; Isaiah 66:24 speaks of undying worms and unquenched fire. 1 Enoch 10:6, 13; 54:1-6 and 90:24-27 describe a fiery abyss or burning valley for fallen angels and apostates; Daniel 7:10 has a river of fire before the throne.
Greek myth located punishment in Tartarus and the fiery river Pyriphlegethon; the volcanic, sulfurous landscape of parts of Asia Minor made the image vivid.

The devil joins the beast and false prophet in final defeat; the dragon's war against the saints is over. Whether 'tormented forever' teaches eternal conscious punishment (the traditional view) or is apocalyptic language for final, irreversible destruction (conditional immortality / annihilationism, held by some evangelicals such as John Stott and Edward Fudge) is debated, but this debate cuts across the millennial schools.
A great white throne and the One seated on it

Daniel 7:9-10: the Ancient of Days takes his seat, his clothing white as snow, his throne flaming fire, the court sits and books are opened. 1 Kings 22:19 and Isaiah 6:1 also picture the enthroned LORD; 1 Enoch 90:20 and 4 Ezra 7:33 describe the Most High on the throne of judgment.
Roman judges sat on raised tribunals; white signified purity and victory.

White represents holiness, justice and victory. The One seated is God (4:2), though the New Testament also says the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22; Matthew 25:31; 2 Corinthians 5:10); Revelation's shared throne of God and the Lamb (22:1) allows both.

Dispensationalists see this as the judgment of the unbelieving dead only, after the millennium, distinct from the judgment seat of Christ for believers (after the rapture) and the judgment of the nations (Matthew 25) at the Second Coming.
Amillennialists, postmillennialists and historic premillennialists generally see one general judgment of all people at the end, with believers present because their names are in the Book of Life.
Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them

Psalm 114:3-7 (sea fled, mountains skipped at God's presence); Psalm 102:25-26 (heavens perish like a garment); Isaiah 51:6. The phrase 'no place was found for them' echoes Daniel 2:35, where the statue's fragments are blown away by the wind.

The old creation cannot stand before the holiness of God, preparing for 21:1. Whether the old cosmos is annihilated and replaced or purified and renewed is debated; most recent commentators lean toward renewal.
Open books… one of them was the Book of Life; the dead were judged according to their deeds

Daniel 7:10 ('the books were opened'); Daniel 12:1 (those written in the book delivered). Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book (Exodus 32:32-33); Psalm 69:28 prays that enemies be blotted out of the book of the living; Malachi 3:16 mentions a book of remembrance. 1 Enoch 47:3, 81:1-4, 90:20 and 4 Ezra 6:20 picture heavenly books of deeds; Jubilees 30:22 speaks of names recorded as friends or enemies. Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12: God repays each according to his work.
Greek and Roman cities kept citizen rolls; a condemned person's name could be erased from the register, losing civic rights — background also for the promise to Sardis (3:5).

Two kinds of books: records of deeds, by which all are judged, and the Book of Life, which records those who belong to the Lamb (13:8; 21:27). Judgment according to works and salvation by grace stand side by side; deeds are evidence of allegiance.
The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead

1 Enoch 51:1 (earth, Sheol and hell give back what they hold); 4 Ezra 7:32 (the earth gives up those asleep in it); 2 Baruch 50:2; 1 Enoch 61:5 includes those devoured by fish of the sea. Isaiah 26:19.
In Greco-Roman thought those lost at sea and unburied were thought to wander without rest; Hades was both the underworld and its god. Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18).
No one escapes the resurrection and judgment, whatever the manner of death or burial. Death and Hades, personified as the fourth horseman and his companion (6:8), surrender their captives.
Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire
Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death forever; Hosea 13:14 taunts death and Sheol.

Death itself, the last enemy, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26, 54-55), preparing for 'no more death' in 21:4. Its placement after the thousand years is noted by premillennialists as matching Paul's order in 1 Corinthians 15:23-26, while amillennialists see that order fulfilled at the single return.

Postmillennialists (Warfield, Boettner, Gentry, Mathison) read the thousand years as a long, symbolic era in which Christ reigns from heaven and Satan's binding allows the gospel to disciple the nations until the world is largely Christianised; it is followed by a brief apostasy (20:7-9), the one Second Coming, the general resurrection and the final judgment. Some locate the millennium across the whole inter-advent age with a growing golden era; others (like Warfield) see 20:4-6 as the heavenly bliss of the saints during the gospel age. Critics ask how a deceived multitude 'like the sand' fits a Christianised world; proponents answer that the rebellion is brief and its defeat instant.
